items.stem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the associates argue, from first to fifth?
items.explanation: Apply the rules as eliminators. A puts F first and H third — not the required immediate F-H block (Rule 1). B places J fifth, violating Rule 2 (J fourth). C starts with K, violating Rule 3. E reverses the block, putting H before F (Rule 1). D — F, H, K, J, G — satisfies all three: F is immediately before H, J is fourth, and K is not first.

items.stem: If H argues third, then which one of the following must be true?
items.explanation: If H=3, Rule 1 forces F=2. Rule 2 fixes J=4. Slots 1 and 5 remain for G and K, and Rule 3 forbids K=1, so G=1 and K=5. Therefore E — G argues first — must be true. A is false (F=2); B and D misplace K (K=5); C is false (J=4).

items.stem: If G argues fifth, then which one of the following must be true?
items.explanation: If G=5, the F-H block (Rule 1) and J=4 (Rule 2) leave only one valid layout: F=1, H=2, K=3, J=4, G=5. So A — K argues third — must be true. E is forbidden by Rule 3; B, C, and D are inconsistent with the forced layout.

items.stem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?
items.explanation: Only three orders satisfy the rules: F-H-G-J-K, F-H-K-J-G, and G-F-H-J-K. In every one the F-H block places H in slot 2 or 3, so H can never argue first — B cannot be true. K fifth (A), G third (C), F second (D), and K third (E) each occur in at least one valid order.

items.stem: If K argues third, then which one of the following must be true?
items.explanation: If K=3 and J=4 (Rule 2), the F-H block (Rule 1) can only fit in slots 1-2, leaving slot 5 for G. The single valid order is F, H, K, J, G. So C — G argues fifth — must be true. A and D misplace G and H, B places F second (F=1), and E puts H fourth (H=2).

items.stem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the students argue, from first (slot 1) to last (slot 6)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H, J, F, G, K, M

choices.label: B
choices.text: F, G, K, H, J, M

choices.label: C
choices.text: F, K, G, H, J, M

choices.label: D
choices.text: F, G, H, K, J, M

choices.label: E
choices.text: F, G, H, J, M, K

items.explanation: Test each order against the four rules. B obeys all four: F is immediately before G (slots 1-2), H is immediately before J (slots 4-5), K (3) argues before M (6), and F (1) argues before H (4); it is the valid order F-G-K-H-J-M, so B is correct. A places H-J ahead of F-G, so F does not argue before H, violating Rule 4. C puts K between F and G, so F is not immediately before G, violating Rule 1. D puts K between H and J, so H is not immediately before J, violating Rule 2. E ends with M then K, so K does not argue before M, violating Rule 3.

In the first the M-P block fills slots 2 and 3, pushing N and R to 5 and 6; in the second the block fills 5 and 6, pushing N and R to 2 and 3. D also fails there, since M (fifth) follows N (second).

items.stem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K argues at some time before F.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: H argues at some time before K.

choices.label: D
choices.text: F argues at some time before K.

choices.label: E
choices.text: M argues at some time after J.

items.explanation: By Rule 1, G argues in the slot immediately after F, so G occupies F's slot plus one. By Rule 4, F argues before H, and since H cannot take G's slot, H must be at least two slots after F — hence later than G. So B, 'G argues before H,' holds in every valid order and must be true. The others each fail in some valid order: A ('K before F') is false in F-G-H-J-K-M; C ('H before K') is false in F-G-K-H-J-M; D ('F before K') is false in K-F-G-H-J-M; and E ('M after J') is false in F-G-K-M-H-J, where M is fourth and J is sixth.

In the first three M precedes R; in the fourth M (fifth) follows R (third), but there L (first) precedes R, so in every order M or L precedes R, and C must be true. A fails in the fourth order (M after R). B fails there too (P sixth, after R). D fails in the second order, where N is fifth, after T. items.stem: Which one of the following could be the complete selection of candidates for the trial team?
items.explanation: Run the rules as eliminators, one violation each. A puts F and H together, breaking Rule 1. B selects G without J, breaking Rule 2. C selects both K and L, breaking Rule 3. D includes neither H nor M, breaking Rule 4. E — G, H, J, L — satisfies all four: F is absent so Rule 1 is idle, G is accompanied by J, only L of the K/L pair appears, and H covers Rule 4.

items.stem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least one of F and H is selected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If K is selected, then M is selected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exactly one of G and M is selected.

items.explanation: J is forced, and the derivation is the game's central inference. Suppose J were out. Rule 2's contrapositive then puts G out as well. The four selections would have to come from F, H, K, L, and M — but Rule 1 allows at most one of F and H, and Rule 3 allows at most one of K and L, so that pool yields at most three. Four is impossible, so J is always selected. Each other choice has a counterexample: G, H, J, K excludes M (refuting A) and includes K without M (refuting C); G, J, K, M contains neither F nor H (refuting B) and contains both G and M (refuting E).

items.stem: If F is selected, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exactly two of G, K, and L are selected.

items.explanation: Chain from F. Rule 1 puts H out, and Rule 4 then forces M in — that is A, and it settles the question. Confirming the rest: with F, J (always selected) and M taking three of the four places, exactly one slot remains for G, K, or L, so no one of B, C, or D is forced, and E is not merely unforced but impossible. The three valid selections containing F are F-G-J-M, F-J-K-M, and F-J-L-M; M appears in all three.

items.stem: If M is not selected, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither G nor H is selected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both G and H are selected.

items.explanation: With M out, Rule 4 forces H in, and Rule 1's contrapositive then puts F out. J is always selected. Two of the four places are filled by H and J, and the remaining candidates are G, K, and L — of which Rule 3 permits at most one of K and L. Two more places therefore require G plus exactly one of K or L. So G and H are both selected: E. The only selections with M out are G-H-J-K and G-H-J-L, which refute A directly and refute B, C, and D by exhibiting one of each pair.

items.stem: What is the greatest number of the candidates F, H, K, and L that can be selected for the team?
items.explanation: Two, and both halves of the answer need showing. Rule 1 allows at most one of F and H; Rule 3 allows at most one of K and L; so at most two of the four can ever appear together — three is impossible, which rules out D and E. Two is achieved: F, J, K, M is a valid selection containing F and K. That witness also rules out A and B, which understate what the rules permit.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be an accurate schedule of the presentations, from first to fifth, with the room for each?

choices.label: A
choices.text: R: Belfry; Q: Atrium; S: Atrium; T: Belfry; W: Belfry

choices.label: B
choices.text: S: Atrium; Q: Belfry; R: Atrium; T: Belfry; W: Atrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Q: Belfry; S: Belfry; R: Atrium; T: Belfry; W: Atrium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Q: Atrium; S: Atrium; T: Belfry; W: Atrium; R: Atrium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Q: Belfry; W: Atrium; S: Atrium; T: Belfry; R: Belfry

items.explanation: B satisfies every condition: Q precedes R, T is in the Belfry, S is not, the third presentation (R) is in the Atrium, W follows T in the Belfry, and R and W are both in the Atrium. A puts R before Q, violating condition 1. C puts S in the Belfry with T, violating condition 3. D gives the third slot to T in the Belfry, violating condition 4. E splits R and W between the two rooms, violating condition 6.

items.stem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Q is presented in the Atrium.

choices.label: B
choices.text: R is presented in the Belfry.

choices.label: D
choices.text: W is presented at some time after T.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exactly two presentations are given in the Atrium.

items.explanation: Condition 2 puts T in the Belfry and condition 4 requires the third presentation to be in the Atrium, so T cannot occupy slot three — C. Both rooms remain open to Q (A) and to R (B), since only T and S are pinned. D fails on the schedule S, Q, W, R, T, where W comes before T. E fixes a count the rules leave free: the Atrium can hold as few as one presentation (S alone) or as many as four.

items.stem: What is the maximum number of presentations that can be given in the Belfry?
items.explanation: Four, so D. The ceiling has two halves. S can never join the Belfry: condition 2 puts T there and condition 3 keeps S out of T's room, so S is always in the Atrium and five is impossible, which disposes of E. Four is reached by the schedule Q(Belfry), T(Belfry), S(Atrium), R(Belfry), W(Belfry): Q precedes R, the third presentation is in the Atrium, W follows R in the Belfry, and R and W share a room. That witness rules out A, B and C, which all understate what the rules permit.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate list of the presentations given in the Atrium?
items.explanation: Condition 2 keeps T in the Belfry, which eliminates A and D outright. Condition 6 makes R and W a pair, so a list containing one without the other is impossible: that is B and C. E survives and is realized by Q(Belfry), T(Belfry), W(Atrium), R(Atrium), S(Atrium), which meets every condition.

items.stem: Which one of the following, if substituted for the condition that S and T are not presented in the same room, would have the same effect in determining the schedule of presentations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: S is presented in the Atrium.

choices.label: B
choices.text: S and W are presented in the same room.

choices.label: C
choices.text: S and R are not presented in the same room.

choices.label: D
choices.text: T is not presented in the Atrium.

choices.label: E
choices.text: S is presented at some time before T.

items.explanation: Condition 2 already fixes T in the Belfry, so 'S is not in T's room' says no more and no less than 'S is in the Atrium' — A reproduces the original schedule set exactly. B ties S to W and so bars arrangements the original allows, such as S in the Atrium with W in the Belfry. C does the same with R. D merely restates condition 2 and therefore drops the constraint on S altogether, admitting schedules with S in the Belfry. E is an ordering rule that neither implies nor is implied by a room rule.

items.stem: If S is presented first, which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: D
choices.text: W is presented either third or fifth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exactly two presentations are given in the Belfry.

items.explanation: With S first, condition 5 leaves W only two homes. W cannot be second, because the first presentation is S in the Atrium; W cannot be fourth, because the third presentation is in the Atrium by condition 4. Slots three and five are both reachable, so D must be true. A and B are each possible and neither is forced — the second slot may go to Q or to T. C happens on S, Q, W, T, R but fails on S, Q, R, T, W. E is not fixed: T may be the only presentation in the Belfry.

items.stem: Which one of the following, if substituted for the condition that K does not argue first, would have the same effect in determining the order in which the associates argue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: K argues at some time after G.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Either F or G argues first.

choices.label: E
choices.text: K does not argue immediately before J.

items.explanation: The other two conditions leave F-H as a block with J fourth, so only four orders survive them: F, H, G, J, K; F, H, K, J, G; G, F, H, J, K; and K, F, H, J, G. The first slot can therefore hold only F, G or K, which makes 'K does not argue first' and 'either F or G argues first' the same rule — C. A is stronger than the original: it also bars F, H, K, J, G, where K argues before G. B and D are weaker in the same way, each admitting K, F, H, J, G, the order the original exists to exclude. E both admits that order and bars F, H, K, J, G, so it matches the original in count but not in content.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be an accurate assignment of clients to attorneys?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perez: F, J; Rao: G, H; Suzuki: K, L

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perez: F, H, J; Rao: G, K; Suzuki: L

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perez: F, G, J; Rao: H; Suzuki: K, L

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perez: F, J, K, L; Rao: H; Suzuki: G

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perez: F, K, L; Rao: G, H; Suzuki: J

items.explanation: D breaks no condition: Perez has four clients to Suzuki's one, F and G are apart, H is with Rao and J is with Perez, and K and L are together. A gives Perez and Suzuki two clients each, violating condition 1. B splits K from L, violating condition 4. C puts F and G together, violating condition 2. E assigns H to Rao without assigning J to Perez, violating condition 3.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be an accurate list of the number of clients assigned to Perez, to Rao, and to Suzuki, respectively?
items.explanation: Condition 1 requires Perez to have strictly more clients than Suzuki, which eliminates A, C and D at a glance. E gives Suzuki none, and the setup requires every attorney to have at least one. B survives, and is realized by Perez: F, H, J; Rao: G; Suzuki: K, L — F and G are apart, K and L are together, and condition 3 stays idle because H is not with Rao.

items.stem: If H is assigned to Rao, which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: B
choices.text: K and L are assigned to Rao.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rao is assigned exactly one client.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suzuki is assigned exactly one client.

items.explanation: H with Rao forces J to Perez by condition 3. Suzuki must then have at least one client and cannot have two: with H and J spoken for, the only pairs left to give Suzuki are drawn from F, G, K and L, and K and L travel together, which would leave Perez with at most two clients against Suzuki's two, breaking condition 1. So Suzuki has exactly one — E. F and G may be assigned either way round, which disposes of A and C. B and D describe arrangements that are possible but not forced: K and L may sit with Perez instead, leaving Rao with H alone.

items.stem: If K and L are assigned to Suzuki, which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rao is assigned exactly two clients.

items.explanation: Suzuki now has two, so condition 1 gives Perez at least three, drawn from F, G, H and J. Condition 2 keeps F and G apart, so Perez's three must include both H and J and exactly one of F and G — and every one of those arrangements leaves Rao the other of F and G. J is therefore with Perez in each: A. E fails on the same count, since H is with Perez. D is false: Rao has exactly one. B and C are each true in one of the two arrangements and false in the other.

items.stem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: D
choices.text: K and L are assigned to Suzuki.

choices.label: E
choices.text: H and J are assigned to the same attorney.

items.explanation: Suzuki with three leaves three clients for Perez and Rao together, and condition 1 then demands that Perez have four or more — impossible. So C cannot be true. Each of the others is realized: Perez: F, J, K, L; Rao: H; Suzuki: G gives A. Perez: F, J; Rao: H, K, L; Suzuki: G gives B. Perez: F, H, J; Rao: G; Suzuki: K, L gives D, and gives E as well, since H and J sit together with Perez there.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be an accurate schedule of the depositions, from day 1 through day 7?

choices.label: A
choices.text: L, T, M, P, N, R, S

choices.label: B
choices.text: L, T, M, N, R, P, S

choices.label: C
choices.text: L, T, S, M, N, P, R

choices.label: D
choices.text: T, L, M, N, P, R, S

choices.label: E
choices.text: L, T, M, N, P, R, S

items.explanation: E meets every condition: N precedes P, M on day 3 and R on day 6 have exactly two depositions between them, S is last, and T follows L immediately. A deposes P before N, violating condition 1. B puts M on day 3 and R on day 5, with only one deposition between them, violating condition 2. C deposes S third, violating condition 3. D puts T before L, violating condition 4.

items.stem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: E
choices.text: R is deposed at some time before M.

items.explanation: Condition 4 puts L immediately before T, so something always precedes T and T is never first — A. Each of the others could be true and none is forced. L, T, M, N, P, R, S deposes S seventh and M third; R, L, T, M, N, P, S deposes M fourth, puts L second and deposes R before M; and S, L, T, M, N, P, R deposes S first and M before R. Condition 2 fixes the gap between M and R but not their order.

items.stem: If S is deposed first, which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: C
choices.text: M is deposed at some time before R.

choices.label: D
choices.text: T is deposed no earlier than third.

items.explanation: With day 1 taken by S, L can be no earlier than day 2, and condition 4 puts T on the day after L — so T falls on day 3 or later, which is D. A, B, C and E are each possible and none is forced: S, L, T, M, N, P, R has L second and R seventh, while S, M, L, T, R, N, P has L third, R fifth, and M before R. S, L, T, M, N, P, R also puts P sixth, and S, N, P, M, L, T, R puts P third.

items.stem: If N is deposed first, which one of the following must be true?
items.explanation: Condition 3 allows S only day 1 or day 7, and N has taken day 1, so S is last — E. The four schedules that satisfy every condition with N first are N, M, L, T, R, P, S; N, P, M, L, T, R, S; N, P, R, L, T, M, S; and N, R, L, T, M, P, S. L is third in two of them and fourth in the other two, which disposes of A; M is second in one only and R fifth in one only, and P is sixth in two of them but second in the other two, which disposes of B, C and D.

items.stem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: C
choices.text: T is deposed fourth and P is deposed third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: M is deposed seventh and R is deposed fourth.

items.explanation: If T is deposed fourth, condition 4 puts L third, so P cannot also be third: C cannot be true. Every other option is realized by a schedule that satisfies all four conditions. S, N, P, M, L, T, R deposes N second, for A. S, M, N, P, R, L, T deposes L sixth, for B. R, L, T, M, N, P, S deposes R first, for D. And S, N, P, R, L, T, M deposes R fourth and M seventh, for E.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate list of the essays selected?
items.explanation: B satisfies every condition: Q is out, so condition 1 is idle; T is in, satisfying condition 2; W is in and so is R, satisfying condition 3; and V is out, so condition 4 is idle. A selects Q and R together, violating condition 1. C selects neither T nor V, violating condition 2. D selects W without R, violating condition 3. E selects S and V together, violating condition 4.

items.stem: If Q is selected, which one of the following must be true?
items.explanation: Q rules out R by condition 1, and W needs R by condition 3, so W is out too. Three essays must still be chosen from Q, S, T and V, which means all but one of them; since S and V cannot both be selected (condition 4), the three are Q, T and one of S or V — T is in either way, which is A. Those same two selections show that B and C are each possible without being necessary. D asks for four, which the count above rules out, and E asks for the W that condition 3 has already excluded.

items.stem: What is the greatest number of essays that could be selected?
items.explanation: Four, so C. Five would mean leaving out exactly one essay, and condition 1 requires that the one left out be Q or R. Leaving out Q keeps S and V together, which condition 4 forbids; leaving out R keeps W without R, which condition 3 forbids. Six fails for both reasons at once, which disposes of D and E. Four is reached by R, S, T and W: Q is out, T satisfies condition 2, R carries W, and V is out. A is below the three-essay floor the setup imposes, and B understates the maximum.

items.stem: If V is selected, which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Q and R are both selected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither T nor W is selected.

items.explanation: R, V and W is a complete selection that breaks no condition — three essays, V satisfies condition 2, R carries W, and S is out — so B could be true. A is barred by condition 4, which keeps S and V apart. D is barred by condition 1. C is below the floor of three. E is the interesting one: with V in, S is out, so the remaining essays are Q, R, T and W, and dropping both T and W leaves at most Q, R and V — a pair condition 1 forbids, so no selection of three survives.

items.stem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: B
choices.text: R is selected but T is not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: W is selected but S is not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: S is selected but T is not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: V is selected but R is not.

items.explanation: S selected puts V out by condition 4, and condition 2 then requires T — so D cannot be true, and the chain takes two steps rather than one. Each of the others is a real selection: R, S, T and W gives A; R, V and W gives B and also C; Q, T and V gives E.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be an accurate schedule of the volunteers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Monday: B (morning), F (afternoon); Tuesday: C (morning), G (afternoon); Wednesday: D (morning), E (afternoon)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monday: C (morning), G (afternoon); Tuesday: B (morning), F (afternoon); Wednesday: D (morning), E (afternoon)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monday: B (morning), C (afternoon); Tuesday: G (morning), F (afternoon); Wednesday: D (morning), E (afternoon)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monday: B (morning), F (afternoon); Tuesday: C (morning), D (afternoon); Wednesday: G (morning), E (afternoon)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monday: B (morning), G (afternoon); Tuesday: C (morning), F (afternoon); Wednesday: D (morning), E (afternoon)

items.explanation: A breaks no condition: B is on Monday, C works a morning, D and E share Wednesday, F works an afternoon, and F and C are on different days. B puts B on Tuesday, violating condition 1. C gives C an afternoon, violating condition 2. D splits D and E between Tuesday and Wednesday, violating condition 3. E puts F and C both on Tuesday, violating condition 5.

items.stem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither D nor E works on Monday.

items.explanation: Condition 1 puts B on Monday, which leaves Monday one open shift; condition 3 requires D and E to share a day, and a shared day takes both of its shifts. Monday cannot hold them, so D is right. Each of the others is possible and none is forced: B may work either Monday shift; C may work Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday; F may work Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday; and G may work Tuesday or Wednesday.

items.stem: If C works on Tuesday, which one of the following must be true?
items.explanation: C on Tuesday keeps F off Tuesday by condition 5, and D and E need a whole day, which only Wednesday can now supply — so F must work Monday, in the afternoon by condition 4. That is B, and it also fixes B on Monday morning, which is why E is false. C is false too: with C in Tuesday's morning, the Tuesday afternoon shift is G's. A and D each hold in one of the two remaining schedules and fail in the other, since D and E may take Wednesday's shifts in either order.

items.stem: If G works on Wednesday, which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: E
choices.text: D and E work on Tuesday.

items.explanation: D and E need both shifts of one day. B has Monday, and G now has one of Wednesday's two shifts, so the only day left whole is Tuesday — E. The four schedules that satisfy every condition with G on Wednesday divide evenly: in two of them C works Wednesday morning with B and F on Monday, and in the other two C works Monday morning with B beside her in the afternoon and F on Wednesday. A, B, C and D each hold in one pair and fail in the other.

items.stem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: E
choices.text: D and F work on the same day.

items.explanation: The day D works is the day E works, and the two of them fill it, so no third volunteer can be scheduled there — F included. E therefore cannot be true, and seeing it means reading condition 3 as a claim about capacity rather than about D and E alone. The others all occur. B Monday morning, F Monday afternoon, C Tuesday morning, G Tuesday afternoon, D and E Wednesday: that is A. C Monday morning, B Monday afternoon, D and E Tuesday, G Wednesday morning, F Wednesday afternoon: that is B and C together. B Monday morning, F Monday afternoon, D and E Tuesday, C Wednesday morning, G Wednesday afternoon: that is D.

items.stem: Which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: N testifies second and R testifies fifth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: M testifies fifth and N testifies first.

choices.label: D
choices.text: P testifies third and L testifies sixth.

items.explanation: Only four orders satisfy every condition — L, M, P, T, N, R; L, N, R, T, M, P; M, P, N, T, R, L; and N, M, P, T, R, L — and D is realized by the last of them. E is impossible because N must leave room for R after it, and the sixth session is the last. C fails because R second forces N first, leaving M and P to fill sessions three and five around T, which condition 1 forbids. A and B each describe a placement no surviving order contains: with N second, R can only be third, and with N first, M and P must take two consecutive sessions that do not straddle T.
